title: Voiced T ゛— だ ぢ づ で ど

points.name: だ
points.explanation: The syllable だ is the voiced version of た — swap the unvoiced 't' for a voiced 'd' to get a 'da' sound as in 'dark' or 'dad'. だ is one of the most important syllables in all of Japanese because it's the plain (casual) form of the copula 'to be' — the equivalent of 'am', 'is', 'are'. The sentence わたしはがくせいだ means 'I am a student' (casual). The polite form is です (desu), and the casual form is だ. Understanding だ unlocks the ability to make basic statements in casual Japanese and to understand sentences you'll encounter everywhere.
rules: だ = た + dakuten; voiced 'd' before 'ah'.
だ is the casual copula meaning 'am / is / are' — the casual equivalent of です.
Many important words also use だ: だいじ (important), だれ (who), だいたい (roughly/generally).
points.flashcardAnswer: da — like the 'da' in 'dark' (voiced version of た; also the casual copula 'is/am/are')

points.name: ぢ
points.shortDescription: Pronounced 'ji' — same as じ in modern Japanese
points.explanation: The character ぢ is the voiced version of ち, and historically it was pronounced 'di'. In modern standard Japanese, however, ぢ is pronounced exactly the same as じ — both say 'ji'. This merger happened centuries ago, and today ぢ is rare and appears only where a compound preserves the original ち (はなぢ, nosebleed, from はな + ち) — its partner づ works the same way in つづく. Most learners will hardly ever need to write ぢ, but you'll encounter it occasionally in dictionaries and traditional texts. When you see it, just read it as 'ji'.
rules: ぢ = ち + dakuten; pronounced 'ji' in modern Japanese — same as じ.
ぢ is rare and mostly appears in compound words for historical/etymological reasons.
When you see ぢ, simply read it as 'ji' — no special treatment needed.
points.flashcardAnswer: ji — same sound as じ in modern Japanese (voiced version of ち; historically 'di')

points.name: づ
points.shortDescription: Pronounced 'zu' — same as ず in modern Japanese
points.explanation: The character づ is the voiced version of つ, and historically it was pronounced 'du'. In modern standard Japanese, づ has merged with ず — they both say 'zu'. Like ぢ, づ is rare and appears mainly in compound words where the original つ etymologically voiced to づ. The most commonly seen example is つづく (to continue), where つ becomes づ in the second syllable. When reading, treat づ exactly like ず. When writing, you'll almost never need づ unless you're writing one of the specific compound words that use it.
rules: づ = つ + dakuten; pronounced 'zu' in modern Japanese — same as ず.
づ appears in compound words like つづく (to continue) and みかづき (crescent moon).
In modern writing, ず is used by default; づ only in specific etymological cases.

examples.english: to notice / to become aware of

points.flashcardAnswer: zu — same sound as ず in modern Japanese (voiced version of つ; historically 'du')

points.name: で
points.explanation: The syllable で is the voiced version of て — 'd' before the 'eh' vowel, like 'de' in 'desk' or 'denim'. で is another vital grammatical particle: it marks the location where an action takes place ('at' / 'in'), the means or tool used to do something ('by' / 'with' / 'using'), and the cause or reason. For example, としょかんでほんをよむ means 'to read a book at the library' (で marks としょかん as the location of the action). で is also the te-form of だ, connecting it to other expressions.
rules: で = て + dakuten; voiced 'd' before 'eh'.
で as a particle marks location of action ('at'), means ('by/with'), or cause ('because of').
で appears in でる (to go out/exit) and でも (but/even so) — both essential vocabulary.

examples.english: to go out / to exit / to appear

points.flashcardAnswer: de — like the 'de' in 'desk' (voiced version of て; also the location/means particle)

points.name: ど
points.explanation: The syllable ど is the voiced version of と — 'd' before the 'oh' vowel, like 'do' in 'door' or 'dole'. ど is the root of interrogatives: どこ (where), どれ (which one), どんな (what kind), どうぞ (please go ahead), and どうも (thanks / somehow). These 'ど words' are among the most essential question words in Japanese. You'll also encounter ど in どうぞよろしく ('pleased to meet you' — a phrase with multiple important vocabulary words). ど even appears informally as an emphatic prefix: どすごい (super amazing) in casual speech.
rules: ど = と + dakuten; voiced 'd' before 'oh'.
ど is the root of question words: どこ (where), どれ (which), どんな (what kind), どうぞ (please).
The こそあど system: こ=near me, そ=near you, あ=over there, ど=question word.
points.flashcardAnswer: do — like the 'do' in 'door' (voiced version of と; root of question words)

chapterPractice.prompt: だ at the end of a casual Japanese sentence means what?
chapterPractice.explanation: だ is the casual form of the copula 'to be'. わたしはがくせいだ = 'I am a student' (casual). The polite version is です (desu), but だ is what you'll hear in everyday speech.

chapterPractice.prompt: ぢ and づ are voiced versions of ち and つ. How are they pronounced in modern Japanese?
choices: ji and zu (same as じ and ず)
chapterPractice.explanation: In modern standard Japanese, ぢ is pronounced 'ji' (same as じ) and づ is pronounced 'zu' (same as ず). These merged centuries ago. You'll rarely write them, but you'll occasionally see them in compound words.
どこ (doko) means 'where'. ど (do) + こ (ko) = doko. The ど series makes question words: どこ (where), どれ (which), どんな (what kind) — all starting with ど.
でも (demo) means 'but' or 'however'. で (de) + も (mo) = demo. It's one of the most common conjunctions in Japanese, used constantly to connect contrasting ideas.
